patterns_data.what_is_impacting: CT / PPO / ACUTE HOSPITAL / authorization-required inpatient
key_driver_codes: YALE NEW HAVEN HOSPITAL
Craniotomy and Endovascular Intracranial Procedures with MCC

patterns_data.pattern_details: CT PPO acute hospital spend rose sharply and was heavily concentrated at Yale New Haven Hospital. The increase reflects both more inpatient activity and higher paid per admission, with added pressure from craniotomy and sepsis admissions. This is a concentrated provider and inpatient management issue rather than a broad marketwide drift.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: A single provider concentration of this size can quickly reshape CT inpatient cost performance and points to both utilization and reimbursement exposure.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Run a joint UM and network review of Yale New Haven PPO inpatient cases, focusing on authorization-required neurosurgery and sepsis admissions, level of care, and contract terms.
evidence_summary: CT PPO acute hospital spend increased about $14.5M.
Yale New Haven Hospital accounted for about $12.8M of the increase.
Admissions rose by 150 and paid per admit rose by about $17.4K.
Craniotomy cases added about $1.3M and sepsis cases added about $0.3M.

patterns_data.pattern_details: ME HMO acute hospital spend increased because inpatient volume rose materially. The cost increase was driven by about 320 more admissions even though paid per admission fell. This points to an admission growth problem more than a pricing problem.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: If admission growth continues, total spend can keep rising even when unit reimbursement is improving.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Have UM operations validate the drivers of the added acute admissions in ME HMO and tighten admission management for authorization-required inpatient stays.

Admissions rose by 320 and claims rose by 165.
Paid per admit fell by about $48.9K, confirming the increase is volume-led.
The growth sits in authorization-required acute hospital business.

This looks like concentrated high-severity case mix carrying across the care continuum, not broad-based utilization inflation.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: These cases can create outsized spend through both the index admission and downstream post-acute placements.

patterns_data.pattern_details: A small number of catastrophic IP Med/Surg cases are driving a large share of spend. The pattern is concentrated in rare transplant, complex spinal fusion, cardiothoracic, and immunotherapy-type admissions rather than a broad change in routine inpatient utilization. The correct response is case-level clinical and payment validation, especially where attribution is incomplete.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: These outliers can materially change results even at very low case counts and require different action than standard utilization trends.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Send these cases for case-level clinical validation and payment review, including catastrophic case management and any attribution cleanup needed for unattributed episodes.
patterns_data.validation_reason: The pattern is dominated by rare, small-count, high-cost cases and includes unattributed scope, so case-level validation is required before trend action.
evidence_summary: Rare IP Med/Surg outliers contributed about $8.4M.
One spinal fusion cluster added about $2.1M from 2 admissions.
Another multi-level spinal fusion cluster added about $1.3M from 6 admissions.
A small number of CAR-T and other catastrophic inpatient cases also contributed more than $1.3M.

HMO acute hospital spend rose on higher admissions, children's facility spend also increased, and PPO acute hospital spend rose even as admissions fell because paid per admit increased. This points to multiple business levers inside one state rather than a single isolated cause.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Kentucky has simultaneous UM, site mix, and reimbursement exposure across more than one inpatient setting.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Prioritize a Kentucky inpatient action plan that separates HMO admission management from PPO reimbursement review and includes a dedicated children's facility review.
evidence_summary: Kentucky inpatient patterns contributed about $7.0M.
KY HMO acute hospitals added about $4.3M on 140 more admissions.
KY children's facilities added about $1.2M with paid per admit up about $16.8K.
KY PPO acute hospitals added about $1.5M even though admissions fell by 20 because paid per admit rose about $13.4K.

patterns_data.pattern_details: Texas cost growth is centered on sepsis-related inpatient admissions, with additional pressure from smaller higher-intensity cases and related rehab or alternative facility use. The main clinical signal is more sepsis admissions rather than higher unit cost, while smaller operational clusters show added acute, rehab, and critical access exposure. This is a focused TX inpatient management issue rather than a broad statewide trend across all conditions.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Sepsis-driven inpatient and post-acute growth can compound quickly when acute admission management and discharge planning are not aligned.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Run a Texas clinical and UM review on sepsis admissions and downstream rehab placements, and check whether POS and HMO authorization pathways are steering cases into higher-cost settings.
